answer:
Main analysis complete (script: analysis/nls_time_preference_bmi.py, seeded and verified deterministic across two independent runs).

HYPOTHESIS / ANSWER to "Does increased time preference lead to higher BMI?":
In NLSY79 the only time-preference proxy is the 1989 savings-flow item ("Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989"), and it does predict BMI 1992 in the predicted direction — more patience (saving) → lower BMI, i.e. more impatience → higher BMI — but the effect is small and mostly explained by pre-existing differences, so the data support an association, not a causal effect. Crude (n=8,503, exposure + BMI1992 both observed): savers (code 1) −0.738 BMI units (95% CI [−1.082, −0.393], p<0.001) vs the "no change" reference; no-savings (code 4) +0.572 ([0.207, 0.936], p=0.002); crude obesity prevalence falls monotonically 22.4% → 20.2% → 18.6% → 14.0% (no savings → no change → took out → put in). Fully adjusted OLS (sex, race cohort, 4 age bands from age-1979, baseline BMI-1989, ASVAB mean z, mother's and father's grades, family size; HC1 SEs): put-in −0.245 ([−0.545, 0.055], p=0.109), took-out −0.039 (p=0.80), no-savings +0.077 (p=0.59); joint Wald on the three dummies F=2.20, p=0.086. The pre-registered ordinal patience index (put-in 3 → no-savings 0) keeps the predicted sign: −0.097 BMI units per one step MORE patience ([−0.177, −0.017], p=0.018) ≡ +0.10 BMI units (~0.018 SD) per step LESS patience; saver-vs-non-saver impatience contrast +0.121 ([0.015, 0.228], p=0.026). Obesity logistic (BMI≥30, 1992): saver OR 0.740 ([0.583, 0.939], p=0.013), took-out OR 0.804 (p=0.061), no-savings OR 0.856 (p=0.18) — so the savings contrast is significant on the obesity tail but the ordinal index is not (OR 0.976, p=0.48), i.e. the gradient is driven by the saver-vs-everyone-one-else contrast, not a monotone preference ladder. Missing-data stability (all HC1): indicator n=8,503 / complete-case n=6,578 / MICE m=10 give put-in −0.245 / −0.220 / −0.234, took-out −0.039 / −0.040 / −0.043, no-savings +0.077 / −0.020 / +0.091 — differences ≤0.10 BMI units, so conclusions do not hinge on the imputation choice. Crucial fragility: dropping baseline BMI-1989 the saver effect is −0.530 (p=0.002), but the change-score outcome (BMI1992 − BMI1989, n=8,448) gives +0.019 ([−0.385, 0.423], p=0.93), no-savings +0.196 (p=0.28) — the forward effect vanishes once the baseline level is removed, which is what reverse causality / pre-existing differences would look like. Heterogeneity: effect concentrated in women (put-in −0.323, n=4,278) vs men (−0.084, n=4,225) and in the younger cohort age-1979 14–18 (−0.444, [−0.860, −0.027], p=0.037, n=5,440) vs 19–22 (+0.117, n=3,063); age×exposure interaction on put-in −0.662 ([−1.286, −0.038], p=0.037), joint interaction F=2.17, p=0.090. Other sensitivities keep the sign: drop no-savings (put-in −0.290, p=0.053), log-BMI (−0.008, p=0.14), age linear+quadratic (−0.244), +BMI-1981 control (−0.180), + own income-1989/wealth-1990 (collider-prone, −0.137, n=6,234).

LIMITATIONS: no direct time-preference measure exists (the savings item mixes preference with liquidity — no-savings group median family net wealth $700 vs $21,000 for savers, mean ASVAB z −0.61 vs +0.40); reverse causality only partly addressed by baseline BMI (change-score model shows no forward effect); self-reported weights and no 1989/1992 height (BMI uses 1985 height, fallback converted 1981 height, with the verified feet*100+inches and pounds readings); 30.3% missing weight-1992 and only 13.4% of those missing the savings item have BMI-1992 (attrition rates across savings categories are mild: 78.1–82.4%); cohort/age-secular BMI trend (22.7 in 1981 → 25.2 in 1989 → 26.1 in 1992) only partly absorbed by age bands + baseline BMI; the bmi89 missing-indicator is estimated on only 55 atypical respondents (mean BMI92 31.09 vs 26.11).

payload.answer: Increased time preference is associated with higher BMI in NLSY79, but the association is weak and largely attributable to pre-existing differences: respondents who put money into savings in 1988-89 (lowest time preference) had BMI 1992 about 0.74 units lower (95% CI 1.08-0.39 below) and 26% lower odds of obesity (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) than the 'no change' group, while those with no savings had 0.57 units higher BMI; after adjusting for sex, race cohort, age bands, baseline BMI 1989, ASVAB, parental education and family size the gradient shrinks to -0.25 (95% CI -0.55, 0.06) for savers with an ordinal patience gradient of -0.097 BMI units per step of more patience (95% CI -0.177, -0.017, p=0.018) and no significant difference for 'took out' or 'no savings'; and in a change-score model (BMI 1992 minus BMI 1989) the effect disappears (+0.02, 95% CI -0.39, 0.42). Conclusion: the data support a positive impatience-BMI association (strongest on the obesity margin, concentrated in women and in the younger cohort) consistent with higher time preference -> higher BMI, but they do not support a causal effect, since the signal is proxy-based and vanishes once prior adiposity is removed.
payload.hypothesis: Higher time preference (impatience), proxied by 1989 savings behaviour in NLSY79 ("Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989"), predicts higher BMI measured in 1992 (n=8,503): each one-step loss of patience is associated with +0.097 BMI units (95% CI 0.017-0.177, p=0.018) and non-savers' obesity prevalence is 22.4% versus 14.0% for savers (adjusted obesity OR for savers 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94, p=0.013). The association is modest (about 0.02-0.14 BMI SDs), concentrated in women (put-in -0.32 vs men -0.08) and the 14-18 age cohort (-0.44, p=0.037; age x exposure interaction p=0.037), stable across median-impute+indicators, complete-case and MICE specifications, but it is not robust to how prior adiposity is handled: it is -0.53 (p=0.002) without baseline BMI 1989 and vanishes (+0.02, p=0.93) when the outcome is the 1989-1992 change in BMI, so we hypothesise that impatience raises BMI only weakly and that most of the observed gradient reflects confounding by resources, earlier-life adiposity and reverse causality rather than a causal effect of time preference.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686x61); verified from data that height-1981 is feet*100+inches and weights are pounds, built BMI = 703*lb/in^2 with height 1985 (fallback converted 1981). 2) Exposure = 1989 savings-flow item as 4-level categorical (reference 'no change') per approved primary spec; pre-registered alternative = ordinal patience index (3..0); sensitivity = drop 'no savings'; plus a saver-vs-non-saver impatience contrast. 3) Outcome = BMI 1992 (n=8,503 with exposure), log-BMI and obesity(BMI>=30) logistic. 4) Primary OLS with HC1 robust SEs adjusting for sex, racial/ethnic cohort, four age-1979 bands, baseline BMI 1989, ASVAB mean z, mother's and father's grades, family size; sensitivities with own income-1989/log wealth-1990 (collider-prone), baseline BMI 1981, age linear+quadratic, no-baseline-BMI levels spec, change-score spec, crude spec. 5) Missing data reported side by side: median-impute + missing indicators (primary, n=8,503), complete case (n=6,578), MICE m=10 with Rubin pooling (seeded, byte-reproducible). 6) Sex-stratified, age-stratified and age x exposure interaction models; selection/attrition diagnostics. 7) Tables written to analysis/results_*.csv, narrative in analysis/report.md and analysis/hypothesis.txt.
